item.title: How might Lindsay Clancy’s case have unfolded in another country?
item.description:
A jury narrowly deadlocked on Friday in the trial of Lindsay Clancy, the 36-year-old Massachusetts woman accused of killing her children. Accused is the correct word in a legal sense. But it feels like the wrong one in a general sense, because it is not in doubt that in January 2023 she killed Cora, Dawson, and Callan Clancy, her three young kids. She admits as much. The jurors instead were tasked with analyzing her state of mind. Also not really in dispute is that Clancy was mentally unwell leading up to the killings—she had begged for help from those around her, gone to the emergency room, tried to check herself into a mental health facility, and said she was afraid to be alone. She was prescribed a laundry list of medications. She was, by all accounts, floundering. Did she ultimately plunge into a state of psychosis? Or was she just deeply anxious and depressed? item.title: Germany's far-right AfD eyes historic state victory in Saxony-Anhalt election
item.description:
Germany’s anti-immigration, nationalist AfD looks set to emerge as the dominant party in key state elections this weekend, cementing its rise and reshaping of the country’s politics. Recent polling published by Die Zeit showed, however, that the party will fall short of winning an absolute majority in Saxony-Anhalt. Sunday’s vote kicks off a spate of major elections worldwide in the coming months that each have the potential to drastically alter domestic — and global — politics. While US attention has concentrated on that country’s midterms in November, they will be preceded by presidential elections in Brazil and parliamentary polls in Israel. In January, Nigeria has its own presidential vote, while France follows suit in April and Spain holds general elections in May. — Prashant Rao

item.title: How Gloria Steinem changed the lives of generations of women

For years, when interviewers asked for a favorite quote, I gave them Gloria Steinem’s: “We are linked, not ranked.” She used the line in 2013 as shorthand for her whole political vision. Publicly, Steinem was a figurehead: the glamorous co-founder of Ms. magazine, a totem for second-wave feminism and a bull’s-eye for its detractors, gorgeously inscrutable behind her curtains of streaked hair and tinted glasses. Privately, she was a workhorse: someone who hid behind her accessories, felt she’d come to the women’s movement late (in her mid-30s), and spent much of the rest of her life hustling to make up for it. If these two identities came into conflict—the persona and the person, the superstar feminist who was terrified of public speaking—Steinem, who died yesterday at the age of 92, simply pushed on.
